## Answer

$S(n)=\{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor,\dots,n-2\}$, which gives $(s(5),s(15),s(30),s(69))=(5,70,315,1717)$.

## Reasoning

**Reformulation.** For a perfect matching $M=\{a_ib_i\}$, let $D_M$ be the digraph on $[n]$ with an arc $i\to j$ when $a_ib_j\in E(G)$, $i\ne j$. A set $S\subseteq M$ is forcing exactly when the M-edges outside $S$ span no $M$-alternating cycle, so $f(M)$ equals the minimum feedback vertex set of $D_M$. Hence $F(G)=n-2$ means some $M_0$ has every triple of its edges containing a 2-cycle or directed 3-cycle, and $G\neq K_{n,n}$.

**Lower bound.** Take any $M_1$ with $f(M_1)=k$, and let $X$ be a maximum acyclic set of $D_{M_1}$, so $|X|=m=n-k$. Complete the block on $X$ to a transitive tournament and make the rows and columns outside $X$ full. This only adds edges, so $M_0$ still has the triple property. Label $X=[m]$ in topological order.

- The zeros are $(r,c)$ with $c<r\le m$.
- Let $u_c=M_0^{-1}(c)$. Then $u_c\notin(c,m]$, since otherwise $M_0$ would use a zero.
- For $c<c'<m$, if $u_{c'}\in(c,m]$, then $u_c$, $u_{c'}$ and any $z\in(c',m]$ form a non-cyclic bad triple (here $z$ has no out-arcs in the triangle).

So $u_{c'}\in\{1\}\cup(\text{outside }X)$ for $c'\in[2,m-1]$, and $u_1$ is in the same set. These $m-1$ values are distinct, so $m-1\le k+1$, i.e. $m\le k+2$. This gives $k\ge\lceil (n-2)/2\rceil=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$. Hence $f(G)\ge\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$.

**Achievability.** For any $j$ with $\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor\le j\le n-2$, set $m=n-j\ge 2$ and $m\le j+2$. Take the block $[m]$ with zeros $(r,c)$, $c<r$, and make $j$ extra rows and columns full. A suitable $M_0$ exists: set $u_1=1$, assign the $j$ outside rows to $u_2,\dots,u_{m-1}$, and make the remaining rows and columns match. Its non-2-cycle graph is triangle-free, so every triple is good and $F(G)=n-2$. Every PM has at most $\binom m2$ non-2-cycle pairs, so every acyclic set has size at most $m$, giving $f(G)=j$ exactly.

Also $f(G)\le F(G)=n-2$. Checks: $S(2)=\{0\}$, $S(3)=\{1\}$, $S(4)=\{1,2\}$, $S(5)=\{2,3\}$, the last one verified by exhaustive search that $f=1$ is impossible for $n=5$.

**Sums.** With $L=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$, $s(n)=\sum_{j=L}^{n-2} j$:

- $n=5$: $L=2$, sum over $\{2,3\}$ is $5$.
- $n=15$: $L=7$, sum over $\{7,\dots,13\}$ is $70$.
- $n=30$: $L=14$, sum over $\{14,\dots,28\}$ is $315$.
- $n=69$: $L=34$, sum over $\{34,\dots,67\}$ is $1717$.

ANSWER: (5,70,315,1717)
